{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 places these catalytic domains in distinct families within the Protein kinase-like superfamily d.144.1 (SUNID 56112): canonical protein kinases in d.144.1.7 (88854), aminoglycoside phosphotransferases in the APH phosphotransferase family d.144.1.6 (64411), and phosphoinositide 3-kinases in d.144.1.4 (56171). Their common fold is d.144, Protein kinase-like (56111), within class d, Alpha and beta proteins (a+b). Superfamily membership supports probable common evolutionary ancestry of the catalytic core; fold membership alone establishes architectural similarity, and class membership only broad secondary-structure organization. Family membership indicates a closer evolutionary relationship but does not guarantee identical specificity or regulation.

The shared kinase architecture supports a conserved framework for nucleotide binding and phosphoryl transfer: a bilobal catalytic core with an interlobe active-site cleft, positioning a nucleotide phosphate donor, metal cofactors, and an acceptor. This supports mechanistic relatedness, not identical catalytic details or proof that every member is active; inactive kinase homologs can retain the scaffold.

Substrate identity cannot be transferred across these families. Canonical protein kinases phosphorylate protein residues, commonly serine, threonine, or tyrosine; APHs phosphorylate aminoglycoside antibiotics and can confer resistance; PI3Ks phosphorylate the 3-hydroxyl of the inositol headgroup of appropriate phosphoinositide substrates. The shared core does not establish a particular protein target, antibiotic spectrum or modification site, lipid substrate preference, or physiological pathway. Likewise, canonical kinase activation-loop phosphorylation, autoinhibition, or partner-dependent regulation cannot automatically be assigned to APHs or PI3Ks, nor can PI3K membrane recruitment and regulatory-subunit interactions be inferred for the other families.

Before transferring specificity, require family/subfamily-resolved sequence and phylogenetic evidence, conservation of catalytic and substrate-contact residues, and structural comparison of substrate-binding pockets and loops, preferably using substrate-bound complexes. Biochemical substrate panels, product/site identification, kinetics, and informative mutational evidence are needed to establish the proposed activity. Regulation requires evidence from the full-length domain architecture, regulatory sites and interaction partners, localization or membrane association, and direct biochemical or cellular tests of the proposed regulatory response. SCOPe supplies evolutionary and structural context, not these functional demonstrations. A distant member can guide modeling of the conserved core, but substrate-binding regions and regulatory conformations require appropriately matched templates and independent validation.","evidence_used":["Pretrained biological knowledge","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","mcp__scope__list_scop_children","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.144.1","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.144.1/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.144.1/children?limit=100"]}]}
